title: Judaism: covenant
hook: a people bound to God through Abraham, Sinai and the Torah

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shema, six words that begin with listen. Your line was hear. Did you listen to someone fully, to take it to heart? Day two hundred forty-seven.

Think of the difference between a contract and a marriage. A contract says: if you do this, I'll do that, and if you don't, we're done. A marriage says something stranger: we belong to each other now, through good years and bad, and even when one of us fails, the bond is still there to come back to. Jews have a word for the relationship between God and the Jewish people, and it's much closer to the second than the first. It runs through the whole Hebrew Bible. Today's word: brit.
screen: `A CONTRACT, OR A MARRIAGE?` → `A BOND TO COME BACK TO.` → `BRIT.`

segments.voice: Brit is Hebrew for covenant, a binding promise between two parties. The Torah tells of several. After the flood, God makes a covenant with Noah and every living thing, never again to destroy the earth by flood, and sets a rainbow in the clouds as its sign. Jewish tradition sees that covenant as embracing all humanity. Then Abraham. God promises him descendants as many as the stars and a land for them, and the sign of that covenant is circumcision, brit milah, still performed for Jewish baby boys on the eighth day, which is why many people know the word as bris. Then Sinai, the great one. The people, freed from Egypt, stand at the foot of the mountain. Moses reads them the book of the covenant, and in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation they answer: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey." In Hebrew, naaseh venishma: literally, we will do, and we will hear. The rabbis of the Talmud loved that order. Doing before fully understanding, like people in love who say yes before they know every detail. At Sinai the covenant is the Torah itself, the teaching and the commandments, a whole way of life given and received. And Deuteronomy says it was made not only with those standing there that day, but with those not yet there. Many Jews understand that to include every Jewish generation since. The covenant runs two ways: God bound to a people, and a people bound to God. Jews have argued with it, struggled with it and wept over it for thousands of years. They've also kept it.
screen: `NOAH: THE RAINBOW, ALL LIFE.` · `ABRAHAM: STARS, LAND, BRIT MILAH.` · `SINAI: WE WILL DO, AND HEAR.` · `WITH THOSE NOT YET THERE.` · then, large: `A PROMISE KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one promise you keep. Settle and breathe. Think of a commitment that's lasted: to a person, a family, a friend, a community, a craft, a faith. Not the ones you broke, just one you've kept. Remember how it began, and a hard stretch when keeping it cost you something. Notice what it's made of you. Let yourself feel the weight of it, and the steadiness. The bell holds the time.
Brit. Hebrew for covenant: the binding bond between God and the Jewish people, through Abraham, Sinai and the Torah. Today's word.
Your line: a promise kept. Today, do one small thing that honors a commitment you've made, without being asked: a call, a visit, a task finished. Day two hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Jews understand their life of Torah and commandments as living within the covenant; brit milah, circumcision on the eighth day, marks a baby boy's entry into the covenant of Abraham, and many communities hold a naming ceremony for girls.
